newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Flattening, but mkt said skeptical.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Flattening, but mkt said skeptical.

text.p: U.S. Treasury yield spreads narrowed after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's hawkish Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday, but not dramatically enough for the market to sense a tightening of monetary policy soon, market participants said.
Players said the risk of a hike in official interest rates has increased somewhat, suggesting the recent bond market rally may be over.
The two-year to 30-year spread narrowed to 72 basis points from 76 late Tuesday.

The two-year note's yield soared to 6.08 percent from 5.90 percent while the bond's yield jumped to 6.80 percent from 6.66 percent. But analysts contended that movement of four or five basis points in yield spreads means little to market psychology.

"The curve flattened on Fed tightening threats, but the curve would have flattened 10 to 15 basis points if the market truly believed a tightening is imminent," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.

Yields in every issue across the coupon curve rose 15 to 20 basis points, disappointing those who had anticipated a more substantial flattening of the curve. While Greenspan sparked the initial jump in yields, a portion of the increase came late in the session after a five-year note auction produced a higher-than-expected yield.
Greenspan, in remarks to the Senate Banking Committee, gave a fairly upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy, noting economic prospects were "quite favorable."
But while the Fed chief was pleased with tame inflation, he said he saw an upside risk and warned that the Fed would not be afraid to make a pre-emptive stike to prevent a brisker inflation rate.
But market players do not expect the Fed to raise rates seven times as it did in 1994 and early 1995.
Greenspan's testimony appeared hawkish, but market players said it was more of the same, as Fed officials have been giving the same line since Greenspan's last Humphrey-Hawkins address last July.

"The market is getting weary of the Fed talking (about a pre-emptive strike) and not doing anything," said Steven Wood, director of financial markets research at BA Securities. "It's more of 'put your money where your mouth is.'"
Wood noted that the July fed funds contract rose only to 5.54 percent from 5.44 percent -- "hardly the market pricing in a tightening" before summer.
Players recalled that fears of rate hikes last year led to the bond market pricing in moves that never took place, and, consequently, many investors got burned.

"It's like the 'Boy Who Cried Wolf,' where (Greenspan) threatened once to tighten and the market sold off violently," Dimick said. "Eventually, threats ring hollow. So, the market is not taking the threats at face value but with a grain of salt. The bond market isn't fully ready to embrace the (rate increase) risks. It did in 1996 and the Fed didn't follow its lead."

One head trader at a leading U.S. primary dealership said that once the market fully digests Greenspan's remarks, the yield curve will flatten further, as short-end rates start to factor in a tightening.

For a rate hike to be fully priced in, the two-year needs to be roughly 100 basis points above fed funds, players said. On Wednesday, the spread between the the two-year and fed funds widened to 83 basis points from 65 -- a clear signal the market is a little worried.
"The market has concluded that there is a higher probability that the Fed is now going to embark on a path to higher rates," the head trader said.
Players said that when the market fears a rate hike, Treasury bill spreads steepen.

On Wednesday, the one-year to three-month bill spread rose to 25 basis points, with the year-bill rising to 5.32 percent from Tuesday's 5.20 percent. Meanwhile, the three-month bill increased to 5.07 percent from 5.02 percent.
"Since the tightening won't come immediately, short-dated paper doesn't get hit as much," Dimick explained.

Players said that even with the backup in rates on Wednesday, the market is still viewed as too expensive. A market fully priced for a tightening would require a 6.25 percent two-year note and a bond near 7.0 percent, given just a quarter-point hike, they added.

"I don't believe 25 basis points makes a lot of difference given the size of the momentum built up in this economy," Wood said. When the Fed starts to tighten, he added, "the likelihood of 75 to 100 basis points is quite good."
Much still depends on the next round of key economic reports, which include the National Association of Purchasing Management and government jobs reports for February next week.

Plus, Greenspan gives the second leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on March 5 before a House banking panel. So, players said, it's a good bet there will be few dull days in the U.S. Treausury market over the next couple of weeks.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
